node.label: Louise Audino Tilly
node.date_label: The Rebellious Century, with Charles and Richard Tilly (1975) · Women, Work, and Family, with Joan W. Scott (1978) · Class Conflict and Collective Action, co-edited with Charles Tilly (1981) · Politics and Class in Milan (1992) · “Connections” (1994)
node.description: Louise Audino Tilly argued that women’s work long preceded industrialization and that wages did not automatically free women from family obligations. Women, Work, and Family (1978), written with Joan W. Scott, explained women’s employment through changing economic opportunities, demographic patterns and household relations in England and France. Scott later recalled that the book, written through an exchange of hundreds of letters, became a standard in the history of women, work and industrial capitalism. Patricia Hilden’s 1979 critique countered that many textile workers valued economic independence and challenged comparisons between working-class women and middle-class housewives. Tilly subsequently called for analytical women’s history that could change historians’ general questions (1989); she also disputed Scott’s deconstructionist method. She also co-edited Class Conflict and Collective Action (1981) with Charles Tilly and wrote Politics and Class in Milan, 1881–1901 (1992). Her “Connections” (1994) extended the study of workers and families across India, England and France.
node.representative_figures_and_works: The Rebellious Century, 1830–1930 (1975), with Charles and Richard Tilly; Women, Work, and Family (1978), with Joan W. Scott (later Methuen edition 1987); “People’s History and Social Science History” (1983; reprinted 1985); “Gender, Women’s History, and Social History” (1989; French version 1990); The European Experience of Declining Fertility (1992), coedited with John R. Gillis and David Levine; “Connections” (1994).
node.scope_note: Books were not read in full. Publisher abstracts or opening extracts were read for the 1975 article, the 1989 essay and Scott’s retrospective. Hilden’s displayed notes were read, not the main critique. The Tilly–Scott methodological disagreement is mediated through Varikas’s publisher extract. Selected passages and notes of “Connections” and Cohen’s appreciation were read. Thompson’s and Passerini’s signed responses were read by OCR from an authorized scan; Tilly’s full rejoinder and the respondents’ books remain unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Tilly and Scott coauthored Women, Work, and Family (1978), challenging an account of women’s employment as the expression of growing individualism.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Scott’s retrospective, publisher abstract, final sentence; AHA bibliography confirms original 1978 joint authorship. “exchange of hundreds of letters” describes their collaboration. Full retrospective, correspondence and book unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Louise and Charles Tilly, with Richard Tilly, coauthored The Rebellious Century, 1830–1930 (1975).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Hanagan and Maynes, opening extract, second sentence and 1975 bibliographic reference; AHA bibliography independently lists all three authors. “along with Charles and Richard Tilly” establishes the joint work. Book unread; no individual allocation of arguments asserted.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Gender, Women’s History, and Social History” (1989), as Varikas reads it in 1995, Tilly disputes Scott’s deconstructionist approach for overstating constraint and diminishing explanations of changes in power.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Varikas, publisher extract, final two displayed paragraphs: “overestimate the weight of social constraint.” Read as an attributed scholarly account; the full 1989 English essay and its Italian version remain unread. Both historians’ demand for analytical gender history is retained.

proposed_edges.relationship: In his response to Tilly’s “People’s History and Social Science History” (1983; reprinted 1985), Paul Thompson (1985) disputes her generalization about oral historians and her separation of social relationships from psychological understanding.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Individually signed Thompson response, printed 19–21 (PDF 17–19), freshly read by OCR in the authorized scan: “gross simplifications.” He agrees with part of her programme but rejects a single prescribed method. Tilly’s reprinted conclusion, 16–17 (PDF 14–15), was also read; Thompson’s books unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Responding to Tilly’s “People’s History and Social Science History” (1983; reprinted 1985), Luisa Passerini (1985) argues that actions and social networks themselves manifest subjectivity and that subjective processes can be historically analysed.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Passerini’s signed response, printed 21–25 (PDF 19–23), especially 22–24: “manifestations of subjectivity.” Full response read by OCR; no oral testimony reproduced. Does not assert that Tilly rejects all oral evidence. Tilly’s complete rejoinder was not read.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Connections” (1994), Tilly uses E. P. Thompson’s concern with ordinary people’s agency to frame her own social history.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Primary opening, paragraphs 1–6; notes 1–3 identify The Making of the English Working Class (1963) and other works. “With his work in mind” is explicit. Named inspiration, not complete agreement; Thompson works unread here.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Connections” (1994), Tilly identifies Hobsbawm’s Industry and Empire (1968) as an influence on her research on industrialization.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Primary note 8: “strongly influenced”; note 4 also acknowledges Hobsbawm. Collective credit with Landes and Wolf, not sole derivation. Cited book unread.
proposed_edges.map_label: Industry and Empire as a resource

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Connections” (1994), Tilly names Natalie Zemon Davis among the teachers and colleagues to whom her approach to social history is indebted.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Primary note 4: “owes much”; Davis appears in a list, without a particular work. This establishes an acknowledgment, not formal dissertation supervision or exclusive influence.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Gender, Women’s History, and Social History” (1989), Tilly calls for problem-solving women’s history whose findings change the questions asked by historians generally.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher opening extract, two concluding sentences, printed opening at 439: “analytical problem-solving studies.” Full article unread. This is a methodological proposal, not mere addition of women to an unchanged narrative.

proposed_edges.relationship: With Scott, Tilly questions the opposition between unproductive domesticity and productive employment in “Women’s Work and the Family in Nineteenth-Century Europe” (1975).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher extract, opening paragraph at 36; “women at home” are described as being wrongly assumed non-productive. Original issue January 1975. Joint argument; full article and its quantitative evidence unread. Existing labour roster retained; no individual Tilly edge already exists.

proposed_edges.relationship: As Cohen explains, the collection The European Experience of Declining Fertility (1992), coedited by Tilly, John Gillis and David Levine, links declining birthrates to changing childrearing attitudes and political, economic and cultural conditions.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Cohen, main-text paragraph beginning “Tilly’s co-edited collection,” with note 5; Hanagan and Maynes bibliography confirms all three editors and 1992. “new attitudes” is the limited explanatory claim. Collection unread; contribution is editorial and collectively credited.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Connections” (1994), Tilly links cotton workers’ family and gender relations in India, England and France through industrialization and imperial economic connections.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Primary opening and synthesis, paragraphs beginning “The interaction of pre-factory” and “A web of connections”; note 7 defines the larger project. “ongoing interplay” distinguishes connection from parallel national cases. Selected passages, not the full address or its source books, read.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Working Families (1993), Bettina Bradbury challenges the claim in Louise Tilly and Joan Scott’s Women, Work, and Family (1978) that single women have few competing claims on their time, as Yukari Takai explicitly reports in 2001.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read Takai’s journal text, especially pp. 129–132. The body explicitly attributes the challenge to Bradbury and then tests it against Lowell evidence about single daughters’ domestic and caring duties. This is a documented criticism reported by another scholar, not an inference from a bibliography. Bradbury’s Working Families (1993), p. 142, and the cited edition of Tilly and Scott were not read directly. The 1978 original year is distinguished from the 1987 reprint identified on Takai’s p. 128. The claim is limited to this particular assertion about single women’s time.

proposed_edges.relationship: In A Crooked Line (2005), Geoff Eley welcomes Louise Tilly’s rethinking of work and politics but criticises its continued materialist basis, placing Women, Work, and Family (1978) within that methodological divide.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher’s licensed chapter preview, printed pp. 116–123, especially p. 122. Eley approvingly discusses Tilly’s conceptual questions before stating his reservation and naming the 1978 coauthored book. The edge preserves that qualified assessment; it does not imply rejection of all her findings. The chapter’s numbered endnotes are outside this preview and were not read here. The book’s 2005 original publication is confirmed by its publisher page. The same substantive reservation was also read in the credited journal translation of Eley’s essay in Genèses 7 (1992), pp. 166–167, on Persée; the English publisher preview supplies this edge’s quotation.
proposed_edges.map_label: Questions the limits of Tilly’s materialist framework

proposed_edges.relationship: In ‘Connections’ (1994), Louise Tilly proposes a social history that joins structures, processes of change and human action, combining narrative with causal explanation.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the AHA’s own text of the address, particularly its opening methodological argument. Tilly specifies reciprocal relations between agency and structure and explains why narrative and causal analysis are both needed. This records her stated methodological contribution to social history, not a claim about subsequent adoption. It is distinct from the input’s global-history edge, which concerns connections among textile-producing regions. Reuse the packet source lt_w_connections; no additional source record is needed.
proposed_edges.map_label: Connects structure, change and human action
